summary: Reports actual measurements of mean round-trip times in the ARPANET.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 619 reports measured round-trip delays for ARPANET messages during seven-day periods in August and December 1973. It explains how round-trip time was measured and compares the results by route and traffic conditions.

questions: how fast was the arpanet in 1974
how does rfc 619 define round trip time
subtitle: Measured ARPANET round-trip times from two seven-day periods in 1973.

tldr.problem: The authors wanted measured averages for important ARPANET performance parameters, including message round-trip delay.
tldr.mechanism: They collected seven-day measurements in August and December 1973 and defined round-trip time from a message entering the source IMP's output queue to its RFNM returning there.
tldr.outcome: The report compares averages and tables by hop count, source and destination, and discusses status reports, routing messages, traffic patterns and topology as factors.

facts.label: Measurement periods
facts.value: Seven days in August and December 1973

today: The unit records RFC 619's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. The RFC reports measurements collected in August and December 1973.

sections.title: How Round-Trip Time Is Defined
sections.content:
The authors define round-trip time (RTT) as the interval from when the message is placed on the source IMP's output queue until its RFNM arrives back at the source IMP. The measurement follows a message through the source and destination IMPs and records when the RFNM returns.

This definition does not include source-host processing delay, host-to-IMP transmission delay or waiting for a message number to become available. For multi-packet messages, the measured interval does include waiting for an ALLOCATE when required.
sections.plainLanguage: The report measures the trip from a message leaving the source IMP's queue until its acknowledgment returns there. It excludes some delays inside the source host and before the message is queued.

sections.title: Measurement Periods and Averages
sections.content:
The authors collected data during continuous seven-day periods in August and December 1973. In August, 2,935 messages per minute entered the network and the overall mean RTT was 93 milliseconds. In December, 2,226 messages per minute entered and the overall mean was 200 milliseconds.

IMP status reports had much larger delays in December and affected the overall figure. Without those reports, the December mean was 132 milliseconds. The RFC also provides tables by minimum-hop count, source site, destination site and selected source-destination pairs.
sections.plainLanguage: The average delay was higher in December than in August, even though fewer messages entered the network per minute. Removing status reports lowers the December average, but it remains higher than the August average.

sections.title: Factors That Affect Delay
sections.content:
The authors identify several reasons for differences in mean RTT. More frequent routing messages increased queuing delay; the traffic matrix changed; and the average number of hops increased from 3.24 in August to 4.02 in December when failures are disregarded. Weekly averages can also hide bursts, and host delays can affect the measured interval.

The report says mean RTT generally rises with more minimum hops, but is not strictly increasing with hop count. It also notes that status reports sent to the NCC had large December delays and distorted the overall picture.
sections.plainLanguage: Delay depends on more than distance. Routing traffic, how messages are distributed, the number of network hops, bursts and host delays can all affect the measurement.

sections.title: Tables for Sites and Routes
sections.content:
The report includes a table of mean RTT by minimum-hop path length, separate tables for messages from and to each site, and a table of the three most-used destinations from each site in December. For December, some site tables show results both with and without status reports.

The authors explain that the minimum hop count comes from the static network topology for each measurement period. Actual messages could travel over more hops because of congestion or line and IMP failures.
sections.plainLanguage: The tables let readers compare delays by route length, sending site and receiving site. A route could use more hops than the minimum if congestion or failures changed its path.

references.text: Kleinrock, L. and Naylor, W., On Measured Behavior of the ARPA Network, Network Measurement Group Note 18, NIC 20793.
